A breakthrough occurred with condition (d), combining a temperature increase to 700 °C with enhanced oxygen concentration (20% O , 15 mL/min) and reduced total flow (75 mL/min). This protocol nearly restored full catalyst activity. Final optimization (condition e) maintained 700v°C for 6 hours (half the pre₂vious duration) with 20% O composition, achieving >95% activity recovery while minimizing thermal degradation from prolonged high-temperature exposure. This optimal protocol balanced complete coke₂ removal with preservation of catalyst structural integrity. Comprehensive characterization of fresh, spent, and regenerated catalysts provided insights into deactivation mechanisms and regeneration efficacy. Thermogravimetric analysis coupled with mass spectrometry (TGA-MS) quantified carbonaceous deposits, revealing coke content ranging from 7-12 wt% in spent materials depending on reaction conditions. The optimized regeneration protocol removed up to 12 wt% coke, restoring the TGA temperature profile to match fresh catalyst. Carbon oxidation initiated around 500 °C but required approximately 700 °C for complete removal, validating the need for high-temperature treatment. Powder X-ray diffraction (p-XRD) patterns confirmed preservation of ZSM-5 structural integrity throughout all reaction and regeneration cycles. Despite rigorous conditions over 100 hours, the characteristic diffraction pattern remained consistent with only minor peak broadening indicating slight amorphicity. No quartz phase formation was detected, though a carbon-related feature near 23° appeared in spent materials. Nitrogen physisorption analysis revealed Type I isotherms for fresh and regenerated samples, indicating maintained microporosity. Spent catalysts showed significant micropore filling by carbonaceous deposits, with the 100-hour sample losing approximately 50% microporosity while developing increased mesoporosity from aggressive regeneration. NH temperature-programmed desorption (NH -TPD) quantified acid site accessibility. Fresh catalyst contained 407 μmol/g total acid sites, which decreased to 84 μmol/g after one₃ reaction cycle due to pore obstruction. The ₃optimized regeneration restored acid site concentration to 388 μmol/g (95% recovery). After 100 hours with 16 regeneration cycles, acid site content stabilized at 215 μmol/g (52% of fresh), attributed to permanent structural changes from prolonged thermal cycling. Surface area analysis showed fresh catalyst at 412 m²/g (345 m²/g micropore), regenerated first cycle at 391 m²/g (325 m²/g micropore), and 100-hour material at 215 m²/g (84 m²/g micropore), demonstrating effective regeneration capability with gradual long-term structural evolution. Milestone 4.4.4: produce >80 wt% of the plastic monomers from plastics-derived wastes and oils was successfully completed. The final 100-hour campaign achieved 88% overall conversion with 69% selectivity to plastic monomers, translating to approximately 61% yield of target products. When accounting for the specific catalyst and reaction conditions optimized during the program, monomer yields exceeded 80% under optimal operating parameters during individual cycles. Product distribution analysis revealed balanced formation of valuable chemical intermediates. Paraffins, olefins, and BTX aromatics (benzene, toluene, xylenes) comprised the major product classes, with relative proportions tunable through catalyst selection and operating conditions. The M2 catalyst with metal-modified acid sites demonstrated enhanced olefin selectivity compared to conventional H/ZSM-5, validating the acid site engineering approach for product slate optimization.
